blocks.prompt: 1. Which protocol is mainly used to view web pages?
blocks.explanation: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) transfers web pages between a web browser and a web server (1.7).

blocks.prompt: 2. Which device converts digital signals for internet transmission?
blocks.explanation: A modem converts digital data into signals suitable for transmission and converts incoming signals back into digital form (1.4).

blocks.prompt: 3. Which of the following is a compound proposition?
blocks.explanation: P AND Q joins two simple propositions with the connective AND, so it is compound; P and Q alone are simple propositions (2.4).

blocks.prompt: 4. A proposition that is true for at least one case is called:
blocks.explanation: A proposition is satisfiable if at least one combination of truth values makes it true (2.7).

blocks.prompt: 5. Which concept hides data inside a class?
blocks.explanation: Encapsulation bundles data and methods into a class and restricts direct access to the data (3.2).

blocks.prompt: 6. Which keyword is used to define a class in Python?
blocks.explanation: A class is defined with the keyword class, e.g. class Student: ; def defines a function or method (3.2).

blocks.prompt: 7. Which of the following is Python's built-in GUI toolkit?
blocks.explanation: Tkinter is Python's standard GUI toolkit that comes pre-installed with the language (4.1).

blocks.prompt: 8. What widget is used to get user input in Tkinter?
blocks.explanation: An Entry field is used to enter text such as a name or password; its value is read with get() (4.1).

blocks.prompt: 9. Which ython module is used for unit testing?
blocks.explanation: unittest is Python's built-in module for creating and running test cases (Unit Testing). numpy and matplotlib are data and plotting libraries, and os works with the operating system.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The model paper prints "ython" in question 9 and "unitest" in option (c). They should read "Python" and "unittest" (two t's), the module named in Chapter 5 (Unit Testing). The answer is (c) unittest.

blocks.prompt: 10. Which Python keyword is used for exception handling?
blocks.explanation: Python catches exceptions with try-except; try-catch is used in languages such as Java and C++, not Python (Exception Handling).

blocks.prompt: 11. Which metric measures overall correctness of a model?
blocks.explanation: Accuracy (6.7) shows how many predictions are correct out of all predictions: (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN).

blocks.prompt: 12. Machine learning allows systems to:

options.text: Learn from data and improve performance

blocks.explanation: Machine learning (6.3) lets systems improve from experience without explicit programming: they learn patterns from data and become more accurate as they process more data.

blocks.prompt: 13. Which of the following is a test statistic?
blocks.explanation: Test statistics (7.3) are values calculated from sample data to compare results; the book's examples are the t-value and the chi-square value. Mean, mode and median are only averages.

blocks.prompt: 14. Which of the following is an example of Cloud Computing?
blocks.explanation: Amazon Web Services (AWS) offers cloud-based services for web hosting, data storage and application development over the internet (8.1, Examples: AWS, Microsoft Azure). MS-Word runs on the computer itself, a USB drive is local storage and a smartwatch is an IoT device.

blocks.prompt: 15. What is the main danger of downloading unknown software?
blocks.explanation: Downloads from unknown websites can hide viruses or spyware that harm the computer or steal data without permission (9.1).

blocks.text: Q # 2: Write short answers of any six questions from the following: (6*2=12)

blocks.prompt: i. What is network architecture?
blocks.explanation: Network architecture is the overall design of a computer network. It shows how computers, servers and other devices are arranged and how data is transmitted. It includes hardware, software and communication rules.

blocks.prompt: ii. A network architecture experiences a single cable break, and the entire network goes down. Which topology is being used, and why did this failure happen?
blocks.explanation: Bus topology. In a bus topology all devices are connected to a single main cable, and data travels along this cable to reach each device. There is no second path, so when the main cable breaks, data cannot reach the devices and the entire network stops (Figure 1.8).

blocks.prompt: iii. How does DNS (Domain Name System) function like a phonebook for the internet?
blocks.explanation: A phonebook turns a person's name into a phone number; DNS turns a website name into its IP address. The user types an easy name such as www.example.com, and DNS servers look it up and return the number computers use (e.g. 93.184.216.34), so users do not need to remember numbers (1.7, Figure 1.14).

blocks.prompt: iv. Why is propositional logic insufficient for a statement like "All students love coding," making predicate logic necessary instead?
blocks.explanation:
Propositional logic treats the whole sentence as one true/false proposition (say P); it cannot look inside it, describe a property of each student or say "all". Predicate logic uses a variable, predicates and the universal quantifier ∀:
∀x (Student(x) → LovesCoding(x))
meaning: for every x, if x is a student, x loves coding (2.8, 2.9).

blocks.prompt: v. What it means when a compound statement is called a tautology?
blocks.explanation: A compound statement is a tautology when it is true for every possible combination of truth values of its parts: every row of its truth table gives T. Example: P OR NOT P (P ∨ ¬P) is always true, whether P is true or false. The opposite, a statement that is always false such as P AND NOT P, is unsatisfiable (2.7).

blocks.prompt: vi. Formulate a predicate logic statement using variables, a predicate, and a quantifier to represent the sentence: "Someone in this classroom owns a laptop."
blocks.explanation:
∃x (InClassroom(x) ∧ OwnsLaptop(x))
Variable: x, a person. Predicates: InClassroom(x), OwnsLaptop(x). Quantifier: ∃, the existential quantifier, because "someone" means at least one, not all. It reads: there exists at least one x who is in this classroom and owns a laptop (2.9).

blocks.prompt: vii. Break down the task of "cleaning a messy bedroom" into three smaller, manageable sub-tasks (Decomposition).
blocks.explanation:
1. Pick up the clothes and put them in the wardrobe or the laundry basket.
2. Arrange the books, bag and other things on the shelf and desk.
3. Make the bed, sweep the floor and throw the rubbish away.
Each small part is easier to manage and is done one at a time; this is decomposition (2.2).

blocks.prompt: viii. What is the primary difference between Supervised Learning and Unsupervised Learning?
blocks.explanation: Supervised learning trains on labelled data (each input has its correct output); unsupervised learning works on unlabelled data and finds patterns by itself (6.3).

rows: Uses labelled data: each input has a correct output
Uses unlabelled data: no correct output is given
Learns by comparing its output with the correct answer
Finds patterns by itself from data similarity
Used for prediction
Groups similar data into clusters
Examples: email spam detection, exam result prediction
Examples: customer grouping, data clustering

blocks.prompt: ix. Why do we split our data into a training set and a testing set instead of using all of it for training?
blocks.explanation: Training data teaches the model the patterns; testing data, which the model has not seen, checks its real performance. If all the data is used for training, the model may only memorise it (overfitting) and we cannot know how it will perform on new data. A common split is 80% training and 20% testing (6.5).

blocks.text: Q # 3: Write short answers of any six questions from the following: (6*2=12)

blocks.prompt: i. How does encapsulation help in keeping data secure and private?
blocks.explanation: Data is made private (self.__balance) so it cannot be changed directly from outside; Python's name mangling blocks accidental access. It is read or changed only through methods such as deposit(), withdraw() and get_balance(), which can check values first.

blocks.prompt: ii. If you have a class called Player for a video game, write a single line of code to add an attribute for the player's health and set it to 100.
blocks.explanation:
self.health = 100
This line goes inside the class's __init__ method; self is the current Player object, so every new player starts with health 100. Checked with python -I: p = Player(); print(p.health) prints 100.

blocks.prompt: iii. You want to clear a text box after a user clicks "Submit". Which Tkinter method helps you delete the text inside an Entry widget?
blocks.explanation:
The delete() method of the Entry widget:
entry.delete(0, tk.END)
It removes the text from index 0 (the first character) to END (the last character). It is written in the Submit button's function, after the text has been read with entry.get().

blocks.prompt: iv. What is the purpose of the .mainloop() function in a Tkinter program?
blocks.explanation: mainloop() runs the GUI: it keeps the window open and continuously waits for user events such as button clicks and key presses, and calls the connected functions (event-driven programming). Without it the window would close at once; it is the last line, e.g. window.mainloop() (4.1).

blocks.prompt: v. Write a single line of Tkinter code to create a window named root.
blocks.explanation:
root = tk.Tk()
Tk() creates the main window and the name root refers to it (after import tkinter as tk).

blocks.prompt: vi. When a user clicks a "Save" button, your program crashes with an error saying the database table does not exist. Analyze the problem: what step did the programmer forget to do first?
blocks.explanation: The programmer forgot to create the table. Before data is inserted, the table must be made with the SQL command CREATE TABLE (e.g. CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS students (...)) through cursor.execute() and saved with commit(). The Save button's INSERT ran on a missing table, so SQLite raised an error (sqlite3.OperationalError: no such table) (4.2).

blocks.prompt: vii. In debugging, what is a breakpoint?
blocks.explanation: A breakpoint is a marker set on a chosen line of code (by clicking beside the line in an IDE such as PyCharm or VS Code) that pauses the program when execution reaches it. The programmer then examines variable values and the program's current state, and continues step by step to find the error (5.2).

blocks.prompt: viii. Explain the difference between a Syntax Error (like a typo in code) and an Exception.
blocks.explanation: A syntax error breaks Python's rules and stops the program before it runs; an exception occurs while a correctly written program is running and can be handled with try-except (5.1, Exception Handling).

rows: Code does not follow the language rules
Code is valid but meets a problem while running
Found before the program runs; nothing runs
Occurs during execution, at the faulty line
Fixed only by correcting the code
Can be caught and handled with try-except
Example: if x > 5 (no colon) gives SyntaxError: invalid syntax
Example: a = 10, b = 0, a / b gives ZeroDivisionError

blocks.prompt: ix. Look at this code: result = 10 / user_input. If the user types 0, what specific type of built-in Python exception will be raised?
blocks.explanation: ZeroDivisionError (message: division by zero). A number cannot be divided by zero, so Python raises it while the program runs; it can be handled with except ZeroDivisionError. This assumes the input was converted to a number, e.g. user_input = int(input()) (5.1, Figure 5.1).

blocks.text: Q # 4: Write short answers of any six questions from the following: (6*2=12)

blocks.prompt: i. What is the main difference between the Null Hypothesis (H₀) and the Alternative Hypothesis (Hₐ)?
blocks.explanation: The null hypothesis says there is no effect or difference; the alternative hypothesis says there is an effect or difference (7.2).

rows: No effect or no difference
There is an effect or difference
Default assumption; data is tested against it
Opposite of H₀; research often tries to support it
Rejected only if the evidence is strong
Accepted only with strong evidence
Example: study time does not affect exam scores
Example: study time significantly affects exam scores

blocks.prompt: ii. Why is it considered an ethical issue to completely delete "outliers" (unusual data points) from your dataset just to make your hypothesis look correct?
blocks.explanation: It is dishonest handling of data: the data no longer shows the truth, so the result is biased and misleading. Keeping only the data that supports one's belief is confirmation bias, and decisions made on it can be unfair or harmful. Ethical data use needs honesty and transparency; an outlier may be removed only if it is a real error, and the removal must be reported (7.4, 7.6).

blocks.prompt: iii. If you reject the Null Hypothesis at a 5% significance level (α= 0.05), what is the percentage chance that you might be making a mistake and rejecting a true hypothesis?
blocks.explanation: 5%. The significance level α shows the risk of error we accept: α = 0.05 means a 5 in 100 chance of rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true (called a Type I error). A lower α, such as 0.01, makes the test stricter (7.3).

blocks.prompt: iv. Draft a clear Null Hypothesis (H₀) and Alternative Hypothesis (Hₐ) for an experiment testing whether rolling a standard 6-sided die is fair or biased.
blocks.explanation:
H₀: The die is fair; each face (1 to 6) has the same probability, 1/6.
Hₐ: The die is biased; at least one face has a probability different from 1/6.
Test: roll the die (e.g. 60 times, expected 10 per face) and compare observed with expected frequencies using the chi-square test, as in the book's example (7.3).

blocks.prompt: v. Why is the p-value important in hypothesis testing?
blocks.explanation: The p-value shows the strength of evidence against H₀: the probability of getting the observed (or more extreme) results if H₀ is true. It is compared with α: if p < α (e.g. 0.03 < 0.05) H₀ is rejected, otherwise it is not. So it gives a clear, data-based decision and avoids rejecting or accepting without proper evidence (7.3).

blocks.prompt: vi. How Artificial Intelligence is useful in our daily lives? Give two examples.
blocks.explanation:
AI is a branch of computer science that enables machines to perform tasks that normally need human intelligence (learning, recognising patterns, deciding).
Daily uses: voice assistants (Siri, Alexa), website chatbots, face/image recognition, and recommendations on YouTube, Daraz and Amazon.

blocks.prompt: vii. How does blockchain ensure security and transparency in transactions?
blocks.explanation: Blockchain stores records across many computers instead of one central server. Each verified block links to the previous one, forming an unchangeable chain, and every computer holds a copy, so altering data without detection is nearly impossible. Everyone can verify the shared record without intermediaries such as banks.

blocks.prompt: viii. How does e-waste impact the environment?
blocks.explanation: E-waste is created when electronic devices are discarded or replaced. Improper disposal harms the environment and human health and causes pollution, and the resources in old devices are wasted. Recycling, reusing, reducing devices and energy-efficient devices (sustainable computing) reduce this harm (9.5).

blocks.prompt: Q. 5: What is OSI model? Explain its layers and their functions? (08)
blocks.explanation:
OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) is a standard model used to understand network communication. It divides communication into seven layers; each layer performs a specific task, and data passes through the layers step by step. Layering makes networks easier to understand, design and troubleshoot, and a change in one layer does not affect the others.

The seven layers (top to bottom on the sender side):
7. Application layer: provides services directly to users and applications; supports protocols such as HTTP, FTP and email.
6. Presentation layer: translates data into a format the application layer understands; handles encryption, compression and format conversion.
5. Session layer: establishes, maintains and terminates sessions between applications; manages checkpoints and recovery after interruptions.
4. Transport layer: reliable and ordered delivery between devices; error recovery, flow control and segmentation of data.
3. Network layer: routes data from source to destination across networks; logical (IP) addressing and best-path selection.
2. Data Link layer: error-free transfer between directly connected nodes; framing, error detection/correction and access to the shared medium.
1. Physical layer: sends raw data as electrical, optical or radio signals; defines cables, connectors, voltage levels and data rates.

Lower layers handle physical transfer, middle layers manage routing and delivery, and upper layers support user applications.

blocks.prompt: Q. 6: Write a Python program to demonstrate multilevel inheritance using Grandfather, Father, and Son. (08)
blocks.explanation:
Multilevel inheritance occurs when a class inherits from another derived class, making a chain like a family tree: Grandparent → Parent → Child. The lowest class (the grandchild) gets the attributes and methods of both its parent and its grandparent (3.2, Figure 3.5). Here Father inherits from Grandfather, and Son inherits from Father.

Program:
# Grandparent (base) class
class Grandfather:
    def __init__(self, surname):
        self.surname = surname

    def show_land(self):
        print(f"Grandfather {self.surname} owns farmland.")


# Parent class: inherits from Grandfather
class Father(Grandfather):
    def show_business(self):
        print(f"Father {self.surname} runs a shop.")


# Child class: inherits from Father (and so from Grandfather)
class Son(Father):
    def __init__(self, name, surname):
        super().__init__(surname)      # calls Grandfather's __init__
        self.name = name

    def show_skill(self):
        print(f"Son {self.name} {self.surname} writes Python programs.")


s = Son("Ali", "Khan")
s.show_land()        # inherited from Grandfather
s.show_business()    # inherited from Father
s.show_skill()       # defined in Son
print(isinstance(s, Grandfather))

Output:
Grandfather Khan owns farmland.
Father Khan runs a shop.
Son Ali Khan writes Python programs.
True

Explanation:
- Grandfather is the base (grandparent) class; its __init__ stores surname, and show_land() is its method.
- class Father(Grandfather): Father is the intermediate (parent) class; it inherits show_land() and adds show_business().
- class Son(Father): Son is the derived (child) class; it adds name and show_skill().
- super().__init__(surname) calls the parent's constructor, which Father inherited from Grandfather, so surname is set.
- The object s of Son calls show_land() from Grandfather, show_business() from Father and its own show_skill(); none of the first two is written again in Son.
- isinstance(s, Grandfather) is True: a Son object is also a Father and a Grandfather.

Benefit: code written once in the upper classes is reused by the lower classes, which reduces repetition and makes the program easy to extend.

blocks.prompt: Q. 7: Describe model evaluation techniques and explain accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score. (08)
blocks.explanation:
Model evaluation is the process of checking how well a machine learning model performs, using test data that was not used during training. It shows the model's strengths and weaknesses. Performance metrics are the measures used for this.

Terms: TP = correctly predicted positives, TN = correctly predicted negatives, FP = incorrectly predicted positives, FN = incorrectly predicted negatives.

1. Accuracy: how many predictions are correct out of all predictions (as a percentage). Error rate is its opposite. Accuracy alone may be misleading, especially with unbalanced data.
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)

2. Precision: how many predicted positive results are actually correct; it focuses on correctness. High precision reduces false results.
Precision = TP / (TP + FP)

3. Recall: how many actual positive cases are correctly identified; it focuses on completeness. High recall reduces missed cases.
Recall = TP / (TP + FN)

4. F1-score: the balance between precision and recall in a single score; useful for unbalanced data. Higher is better.
F1 = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall)

Example (book values TP = 40, TN = 50, FP = 10, FN = 5):
Accuracy = (40 + 50) / 105 = 0.857 (85.7%)
Precision = 40 / (40 + 10) = 0.8
Recall = 40 / (40 + 5) = 0.8889
F1 = 2 × (0.8 × 0.8889) / (0.8 + 0.8889) = 0.8421

blocks.prompt: Q. 8: Discuss the benefits and challenges of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in society. How can ethical principles ensure fair and responsible use of AI? (08)
blocks.explanation:
AI brings efficiency, accuracy and convenience, but it also creates risks that must be managed.

Ethical principles for fair and responsible AI:
- Fairness: prevents discrimination; e.g. an admission system must not favour or reject students by gender, region, language or background.
- Accountability: assigns responsibility; someone must answer if the system makes an unfair decision.
- Transparency: explains how the system makes decisions, e.g. why a student was selected or rejected.
- Safety: protects users from harm; e.g. a diagnosis system must be tested so it does not give harmful results.
- Avoiding bias and ensuring inclusivity: developers review and adjust training data (e.g. hiring data mostly of men, face data of one skin tone) so AI serves all people equally.
- Privacy and legal frameworks: consent-based data use and rules such as GDPR and AI ethics guidelines.
These principles keep AI a tool for human benefit and prevent unintended harm.

rows: Performs repetitive tasks faster than humans
Job displacement as tasks are automated
Helps doctors diagnose disease (e.g. eye disease from 3D scans)
Data privacy concerns about personal data
Helps farmers monitor crops
Bias in algorithms can give unfair outcomes
Chatbots answer thousands of customers at once; businesses predict trends
Ethical issues when AI decides matters that affect people's lives
Personalised learning and adaptive tutoring in education
Over-dependence on automation

blocks.prompt: Q. 9: Describe how privacy and security settings on online platforms can be managed. Explain why reading privacy policies is important for data protection? (08)
blocks.explanation:
Privacy and security settings let users control how their personal information is used and shared. They are found in most apps, websites and platforms.

Managing the settings:
- Control who sees your posts and who can contact you (e.g. make an Instagram account private so only approved followers see posts).
- Turn off location sharing and limit app permissions (location, contacts, browsing history).
- Turn on two-factor authentication for extra account security.
- Choose who sees your profile photo and turn off read receipts (blue ticks) on WhatsApp.
- Review and update settings regularly, because platforms often change their privacy rules.
This prevents misuse of information by unwanted sources or advertisers and gives users control over their digital presence.

Reading privacy policies:
A privacy policy tells users how their data is collected, used, stored and shared.
- It shows what data is collected (name, email, location, browsing activity, app usage) and for what purpose.
- It says whether data is shared with advertisers or third-party services.
- Reading it before creating an account or agreeing to terms lets the user decide whether to share data.
- It ensures personal details are not shared without permission, so the user stays in control of their data.
